frames.narration: A greedy algorithm sorts its candidates by a rule, then walks through once and keeps each candidate that still fits. No choice is ever taken back. After the sort that is a single pass: 9,730 comparisons and checks for 1,000 jobs.

Goal: the most jobs with no overlap. Rule 1, earliest start, takes 153 jobs: one long job that starts first blocks many short ones. Rule 2, shortest first, takes 237: a short job sitting between two good ones blocks both. Both sound sensible.

Rule 3, earliest finish, takes 241 jobs, and that is the best possible. Why: take any best schedule and swap its first job for the earliest-finishing one. The swap ends no later, so it overlaps nothing after it, and the schedule keeps its size. Repeat on what is left. That is the exchange argument.

Give every job a weight and the proof stops working. Earliest finish ignores weights and collects 2,460; heaviest first collects 2,689; the optimum is 3,084. The best choice now depends on later jobs, so no sorting rule is right. Dynamic programming tries both options for each job and remembers the best total.

Coin change with 1, 3, 4 and amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1, three coins, while 3 + 3 is two. Over the amounts 1 to 1,000 greedy is wrong for 249. With 1, 5, 10, 25 it is never wrong in that range, which is why the bug hides until the coins change.

Why anyone still uses greedy: for 100,000 with coins 1, 5, 10, 25 it needs 4 steps. The table method behind the exact answer needs 400,000. When a coin set is known to suit greedy, that gap is a bargain; when it is not, it is what you pay for being right.

Greedy as a heuristic: filling a knapsack by value per weight reaches 1,256 against an optimum of 1,263 with 80 items, and 80 against 89 with 10 items. Usually close, never guaranteed. A few greedy rules do carry a proven bound, such as set cover being within about ln n of the best.

Before trusting a rule, ask for the exchange argument. If you cannot give one, try the rule against brute force on tiny inputs: enumerate all 16,384 subsets of 14 jobs and compare. One disagreement means the rule is a guess, not an algorithm.
